Read-only: never edits code. (Tools: Bash, Glob, Grep, Read, LSP, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- architect-sol: Designs implementation architectures: analyzes existing codebase patterns, then delivers a blueprint — files to create/modify, component design, data flow, build sequence, risks, alternatives. Read-only: never edits code. (Tools: Bash, Glob, Grep, Read, LSP, WebFetch, WebSearch)
- claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Glob, Grep, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- code-reviewer-fable: Adversarial code review of diffs/commits/PRs: correctness, security, data integrity, conventions. Verifies each finding before reporting, ranks BLOCKER/MAJOR/MINOR with file:line and concrete failure scenario. Read-only: never fixes. (Tools: Bash, Glob, Grep, Read, LSP, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- code-reviewer-opus: Adversarial code review of diffs/commits/PRs: correctness, security, data integrity, conventions. Verifies each finding before reporting, ranks BLOCKER/MAJOR/MINOR with file:line and concrete failure scenario. Read-only: never fixes. (Tools: Bash, Glob, Grep, Read, LSP, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- code-reviewer-sol: Adversarial code review of diffs/commits/PRs: correctness, security, data integrity, conventions. Verifies each finding before reporting, ranks BLOCKER/MAJOR/MINOR with file:line and concrete failure scenario. Read-only: never fixes. (Tools: Bash, Glob, Grep, Read, LSP, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- codex:codex-rescue: Proactively use when Claude Code is stuck, wants a second implementation or diagnosis pass, needs a deeper root-cause investigation, or should hand a substantial coding task to Codex through the shared runtime (Tools: Bash)

- entire-search: Search Entire checkpoint history and transcripts with `entire search --json`. Use proactively when the user asks about previous work, commits, sessions, prompts, or historical context in this repository. (Tools: Bash)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- feature-dev:code-architect: Designs feature architectures by analyzing existing codebase patterns and conventions, then providing comprehensive implementation blueprints with specific files to create/modify, component designs, data flows, and build sequences (Tools: Glob, Grep, LS, Read, NotebookRead, WebFetch, TodoWrite, WebSearch, KillShell, BashOutput)

- feature-dev:code-explorer: Deeply analyzes existing codebase features by tracing execution paths, mapping architecture layers, understanding patterns and abstractions, and documenting dependencies to inform new development (Tools: Glob, Grep, LS, Read, NotebookRead, WebFetch, TodoWrite, WebSearch, KillShell, BashOutput)

- feature-dev:code-reviewer: Reviews code for bugs, logic errors, security vulnerabilities, code quality issues, and adherence to project conventions, using confidence-based filtering to report only high-priority issues that truly matter (Tools: Glob, Grep, LS, Read, NotebookRead, WebFetch, TodoWrite, WebSearch, KillShell, BashOutput)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- project-structure-validator: Validates project structure against co-location and architecture patterns defined in AGENTS.md (Tools: All tools)

- sol: General-purpose subagent running on Codex GPT-5.6 Sol via the claude-all gateway. Use for heavy implementation, deep debugging, second-opinion reviews, or any Task the orchestrator wants executed by GPT-5.6 Sol instead of a Claude model. Accepts any prompt a general-purpose agent would. (Tools: All tools)
- spark: General-purpose subagent running on Codex GPT-5.3 Spark (fast) via the claude-all gateway. Use for quick mechanical subtasks, bulk edits, and speed-over-depth work. (Tools: All tools)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

- understand-anything:architecture-analyzer: Analyzes a codebase's file structure, summaries, and import relationships to identify
logical architectural layers and assign every file to exactly one layer. (Tools: All tools)

- understand-anything:article-analyzer: Analyzes markdown files using pre-parsed structural data and LLM inference to extract knowledge graph nodes and edges (entities, claims, implicit relationships, topic clustering). (Tools: All tools)

- understand-anything:assemble-reviewer: Reviews the output of merge-batch-graphs.py for semantic issues the script

- understand-anything:domain-analyzer: Analyzes codebases to extract business domain knowledge — domains, business flows, and process steps. Produces a domain-graph.json that maps how business logic flows through the code. (Tools: All tools)

- understand-anything:file-analyzer: Analyzes batches of source files to produce knowledge graph nodes and edges.
Extracts file structure, functions, classes, and relationships using a two-phase
approach: structural extraction script followed by LLM semantic analysis. (Tools: All tools)

- understand-anything:graph-reviewer: Validates knowledge graphs for correctness, completeness, and quality.
Runs systematic checks and renders approval or rejection decisions. (Tools: All tools)

- understand-anything:knowledge-graph-guide: Use this agent when users need help understanding, querying, or working
with an Understand-Anything knowledge graph. Guides users through graph
structure, node/edge relationships, layer architecture, tours, and
dashboard usage. (Tools: All tools)

- understand-anything:project-scanner: Scans a codebase directory to produce a structured inventory of all project files,
detected languages, frameworks, import maps, and estimated complexity. (Tools: All tools)

- understand-anything:tour-builder: Designs guided learning tours through codebases, creating 5-15 pedagogical steps
that teach project architecture and key concepts in logical order. (Tools: All tools)

- access-new-relic-logs: Use when you or the user wants to investigate logs for app.
- access-outlook-business-email: Use when you or the user wants to read, search, triage, or reason about a Microsoft 365 business mailbox, or draft a reply or new email for the user to review and send. This skill never sends — it only creates drafts.
- access-xero-for-px: Full Xero API control for the "Px Internal" Custom Connection (machine-to-machine, single org Pharmacy-Xpress). Use when you or the user wants to read or write Xero data for the PX organisation — invoices, contacts, payments, items, bank transactions, reports, payroll, files, assets. Authenticates via OAuth2 client_credentials and exposes a generic HTTP passthrough to any Xero API endpoint.
- anvil-yaml: Update Anvil app manifest files in `anvil.yaml`, including services, app metadata, and `db_schema`, using the Anvil YAML type reference available to this agent and `anvil --json validate`.
- brand-guidelines: Applies Anthropic's official brand colors and typography to any sort of artifact that may benefit from having Anthropic's look-and-feel. Use it when brand colors or style guidelines, visual formatting, or company design standards apply.
- call-another-llm: Call Codex CLI or Claude Code CLI with a prompt and save the response to tmp/llm-responses/. Use when you need a second opinion, want to offload a subtask, or compare answers across LLMs.
- canvas-design: Create beautiful visual art in .png and .pdf documents using design philosophy. You should use this skill when the user asks to create a poster, piece of art, design, or other static piece. Create original visual designs, never copying existing artists' work to avoid copyright violations.
- chatgpt-pro-browser-query: Query ChatGPT through the user's already signed-in browser session while proving ChatGPT Pro and Extended Pro are active before sending. Use this whenever the user asks an agent to ask ChatGPT, use ChatGPT Pro, compare with ChatGPT, query the ChatGPT web app, or get a second opinion specifically from their ChatGPT subscription instead of the API.
- chrome-control: Shared Chrome DevTools control bridge that owns the single CDP connection so multiple Chrome-using skills run from one Chrome "Allow control" approval. Use as STEP 1 of any skill that drives the user's Chrome (ChatGPT browser query, ChatGPT image generation, future browser-driving skills).
- chrome-devtools-cli: Use this skill to write shell scripts or run shell commands to automate tasks in the browser or otherwise use Chrome DevTools via CLI.
- claude-epic-pr-review: Token-intensive, maximal review of a large pull request or branch. Runs three parallel review streams — a 5-agent Codex xhigh swarm with overlapping coverage, an adversarial multi-agent epic-review workflow, and a fork that validates every existing PR comment after checks pass — then consolidates all findings, auto-fixes valid code bugs in parallel while asking the user about UX / DB-schema / new-file decisions, runs /code-review max + /simplify max, and replaces the PR. Use for large, high-risk, or cross-cutting changes when an exhaustive, deliberately expensive review is wanted.
- claude-fork-mode: Operate in fork-first mode — delegate all work to background forks (the Agent tool with `subagent_type "fork"`) that inherit the full conversation, so heavy, noisy, or parallel work stays out of the main context window and only compact reports return. Use when the user says "fork mode", "use forks for everything", "delegate everything to forks", or wants to preserve the main agent's context by running work in forks.
- claude-team-review-plan-implementation: Launch a large team of agents (Codex, Opus teammates) to line-by-line compare a reference plan against its implementation across multiple repos, extract deviations, validate, fix, verify, triage design decisions with the user, simplify, and create PRs. Accepts a reference file name as its argument.
- claude-workflow-mode: Operate in workflow-first mode — the main agent becomes an orchestrator that routes single-threaded work to background forks (the Agent tool with `subagent_type "fork"`, which inherit full conversation context and share the prompt cache) and routes ALL parallelizable work to the Workflow tool (deterministic multi-agent fan-out). Single serial stream → one fork; anything that can run concurrently → a workflow. TOKEN-HEAVY — this mode scales comprehensively by default, spawning many subagents per task and burning a large amount of tokens — only use it when that cost is acceptable. Use when the user says "workflow mode", "workflow-first mode", "use workflows for parallel work", or wants parallel work orchestrated through workflows while keeping the main agent's context lean.
- client-forms: Create, inspect, edit, style, validate, and convert Anvil client Forms under `client_code`, including Form Python, HTML templates, event wiring, Data Bindings, RepeatingPanel item templates, reusable Forms, theme CSS, and legacy YAML templates.
- client-modules: Edit Anvil client code Python modules under `client_code` that are not form definitions, without touching read-only dependencies or form templates.
- codex-image-generation: Generate or edit images through Codex CLI's built-in image_gen tool, driven headlessly via `codex exec` on the user's ChatGPT subscription (no OPENAI_API_KEY, no browser). Use whenever the user asks an agent to "generate an image", "make an image with Codex/ChatGPT", edit an existing image, produce icons/mock-ups/hero art/social assets, or create transparent-background PNGs. Supports single generate, multi-prompt batch, image editing, and chroma-key transparency. Final images are written to `<cwd>/tmp/codex-image-generation` by default (override with `--output-dir`).
- data-models: Design idiomatic Anvil data models and client/server data flow for new apps, CRUD workflows, Data Tables, model classes, buffering, drafts, Data Bindings, and server methods. Use before choosing an architecture for persisted domain data, when the user asks about Anvil models/model classes, or when deciding whether to pass rows, model objects, dicts, or server-callable payloads.
- doc-coauthoring: Guide users through a structured workflow for co-authoring documentation. Use when user wants to write documentation, proposals, technical specs, decision docs, or similar structured content. This workflow helps users efficiently transfer context, refine content through iteration, and verify the doc works for readers. Trigger when user mentions writing docs, creating proposals, drafting specs, or similar documentation tasks.
- docx: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx files) or Word templates (.dotx files). Triggers include: any mention of 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', or requests to produce professional documents with formatting like tables of contents, headings, page numbers, or letterheads. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, performing find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a 'report', 'memo', 'letter', 'template', or similar deliverable as a Word or .docx file, use this skill. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or general coding tasks unrelated to document generation.
- frontend-design: Guidance for distinctive, intentional visual design when building new UI or reshaping an existing one. Helps with aesthetic direction, typography, and making choices that don't read as templated defaults.
- heavy-swarm-plan: Build a read-only implementation plan for complex, multi-area work and pressure-test that plan with Codex CLI and Claude Code CLI before implementation starts. Use when the task is large, ambiguous, cross-cutting, or risky enough that a normal quick plan is not sufficient.
- implement-good-test-patterns: Use datasette-enrichments as a testing reference and imitate its pytest patterns when adding or restructuring tests. Use when writing tests, improving test structure, or aligning a Python project with good integration-style pytest patterns.
- initiate-smoke-tests: Interactive smoke-test runner. Reset the Neon test branch, patch in the fixtures the tests need, then walk the user through each UI smoke test one at a time via AskUser — the question names the exact app, care home, patient(s), med(s), and action. Forks (`subagent_type "fork"`, full context) do every DB sanity check, doc status update, and bug fix. Use when the user says "initiate smoke tests", "let's run the smoke tests", "start/resume smoke testing", or wants to execute a smoke-test doc against the test environment.
- mailshot-carehomes: Use when you or the user wants to send a single bulk announcement (mailshot) to every care-home portal contact - e.g. a new branding link, a portal change, a service notice. Gathers all care-home recipient emails from the Anvil carehome_portal_users table and the Neon "PX" script-copy table, then drafts ONE email (FROM team@, CC stacey@, BCC every care-home contact + zoe@/paresh@/mandeep@) via the access-outlook-business-email skill. Never sends - it only creates a draft for the user to review and send.
- manage-m365-tenant: Use when you or the user wants to administer the Microsoft 365 tenancy — users, groups, licenses, roles, domains, devices, policies, security alerts, audit logs, SharePoint sites, Teams, and usage reports. Full read/write control via Microsoft Graph.
- mk-feature-plan-mode: Plan-only feature design mode. The user states a feature objective; read-only forks map the existing codebase (data model, screens, modules) while the main agent grills the user via AskUser to lock down every UX edge case and scenario. The locked plan is then reviewed by ~2 parallel Codex agents plus an architecture-review sub-agent; any new gaps loop back to the user. Once locked, it writes a feature_plan_<feature>.html design doc to the cwd (UI screens, schema changes, file-tree of new/changed files, out-of-scope) and opens it in the user's default browser, plus a migration.py (test branch by default, --live for prod) only when the schema changes are not purely additive. Use when the user says "feature plan mode", "plan this feature", "design doc for ...", or wants a reviewable UX/architecture plan before any code is written.
- pdf: Use this skill whenever the user wants to do anything with PDF files. This includes reading or extracting text/tables from PDFs, combining or merging multiple PDFs into one, splitting PDFs apart, rotating pages, adding watermarks, creating new PDFs, filling PDF forms, encrypting/decrypting PDFs, extracting images, and OCR on scanned PDFs to make them searchable. If the user mentions a .pdf file or asks to produce one, use this skill.
- performance-metrics-from-new-relic: Use when you or the user wants frontend performance metrics from New Relic, including Largest Contentful Paint, Interaction to Next Paint, Cumulative Layout Shift, poor distributions, and worst URLs or sessions.
- pptx: Use this skill any time a .pptx or .potx file is involved in any way — as input, output, or both. This includes: creating slide decks, pitch decks, or presentations; reading, parsing, or extracting text from any .pptx or .potx file (even if the extracted content will be used elsewhere, like in an email or summary); editing, modifying, or updating existing presentations; combining or splitting slide files; working with templates (.potx), layouts, speaker notes, or comments. Trigger whenever the user mentions "deck," "slides," "presentation," or references a .pptx or .potx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. If a .pptx or .potx file needs to be opened, created, or touched, use this skill.
- pr-swarm-review: Fetch comments from an open GitHub pull request, then use a single sub-agent to extract every reviewer's substantive concerns and validate each one against the codebase in one pass, and consolidate the verdicts back in the main agent for triage and fixing. Use when the user wants existing PR comments triaged before deciding what to fix.
- quick-smoke-tests: Generate an ordered, dependency-aware list of UI smoke tests for the work just completed in this session. Walk the user through every test using the AskUser tool — one question per test with all details embedded in the question — then validate each reported result against the database. Use when the user says "smoke test what we just did", "let's quickly verify the changes in the UI", or similar after implementation work.
- server-code: Edit Anvil server code Python modules under `server_code`, including server-callable functions, background logic, and server packages, while keeping changes isolated to the app workspace.
- skill-creator: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy.
- sync-global-user-instructions-md: Sync one canonical global instruction file into user-global Codex and Claude instruction files. Use when you need to update the canonical user-global instructions, diff installed global files against canon, reconcile drift, or replace user-global AGENTS/CLAUDE files from the canonical source.
- sync-mcps: Sync canonical MCP server manifests into Claude Code, Codex CLI, and Cursor config files. Use when you need to add, remove, or update an MCP across all agents from one source of truth, or to diff installed MCP configs against canon.
- taste: Reverse-engineer the design taste of any website. Given a URL, captures DOM data and a screenshot via real browser, then runs a 4-step analysis to produce {domain}.md + {domain}.json with practical design tokens (colors, typography, spacing, radii, shadows, grid) AND taste DNA (Trigger → Decision → Reason → Evidence trade-offs explaining WHY the design works). Use whenever the user wants to extract a site's design system, study a competitor's visual language, port an aesthetic to a new project, or generate design guidance for an AI coding agent. Triggers on '/taste <url>', 'analyze the design of X', 'what makes X's site good', 'extract design tokens from X', 'give me X's design DNA', 'build something in the style of X', 'I want my app to feel like X'. Output rejects AI slop ('clean', 'modern', 'user-friendly') in favor of concrete px/hex values and restraint trade-offs. Do NOT use for scraping data, summarizing page content, or tasks unrelated to visual design.
- theme-factory: Toolkit for styling artifacts with a theme. These artifacts can be slides, docs, reportings, HTML landing pages, etc. There are 10 pre-set themes with colors/fonts that you can apply to any artifact that has been creating, or can generate a new theme on-the-fly.
- webapp-testing: Toolkit for interacting with and testing local web applications using Playwright. Supports verifying frontend functionality, debugging UI behavior, capturing browser screenshots, and viewing browser logs.
- windows-computer-use: Drive the Windows desktop UI the way a user can — list monitors/windows, read UIA element trees, click/right-click/double-click, type text, send key chords, scroll, drag, and capture screenshots across multiple monitors and any app type. Use when a task needs native Windows app or OS control beyond the browser (File Explorer, Settings, installers, system dialogs, Office desktop, WinUI/UWP/Win32 apps). For controlling a web browser, prefer chrome-control / the browser skills instead.
- xlsx: Use this skill any time a spreadsheet file is the primary input or output. This means any task where the user wants to: open, read, edit, or fix an existing .xlsx, .xlsm, .xltx, .csv, or .tsv file (e.g., adding columns, computing formulas, formatting, charting, cleaning messy data); create a new spreadsheet from scratch or from other data sources; or convert between tabular file formats. Trigger especially when the user references a spreadsheet file by name or path — even casually (like "the xlsx in my downloads") — and wants something done to it or produced from it. Also trigger for cleaning or restructuring messy tabular data files (malformed rows, misplaced headers, junk data) into proper spreadsheets. The deliverable must be a spreadsheet file. Do NOT trigger when the primary deliverable is a Word document, HTML report, standalone Python script, database pipeline, or Google Sheets API integration, even if tabular data is involved.
- codex:rescue: Delegate investigation, an explicit fix request, or follow-up rescue work to the Codex rescue subagent
- codex:setup: Check whether the local Codex CLI is ready and optionally toggle the stop-time review gate
- feature-dev:feature-dev: Guided feature development with codebase understanding and architecture focus
- astral:ruff: Guide for using ruff, the extremely fast Python linter and formatter. Use this when linting, formatting, or fixing Python code.
- astral:ty: Guide for using ty, the extremely fast Python type checker and language server. Use this when type checking Python code or setting up type checking in Python projects.
- astral:uv: Guide for using uv, the Python package and project manager. Use this when working with Python projects, scripts, packages, or tools.
- codex:codex-cli-runtime: Internal helper contract for calling the codex-companion runtime from Claude Code
- codex:codex-result-handling: Internal guidance for presenting Codex helper output back to the user
- codex:gpt-5-4-prompting: Internal guidance for composing Codex and GPT-5.4 prompts for coding, review, diagnosis, and research tasks inside the Codex Claude Code plugin
- frontend-design:frontend-design: Guidance for distinctive, intentional visual design when building new UI or reshaping an existing one. Helps with aesthetic direction, typography, and making choices that don't read as templated defaults.
- understand-anything:understand: Analyze a codebase to produce an interactive knowledge graph for understanding architecture, components, and relationships
- understand-anything:understand-chat: Use when you need to ask questions about a codebase or understand code using a knowledge graph
- understand-anything:understand-dashboard: Launch the interactive web dashboard to visualize a codebase's knowledge graph
- understand-anything:understand-diff: Use when you need to analyze git diffs or pull requests to understand what changed, affected components, and risks
- understand-anything:understand-domain: Extract business domain knowledge from a codebase and generate an interactive domain flow graph. Works standalone (lightweight scan) or derives from an existing /understand knowledge graph.
- understand-anything:understand-explain: Use when you need a deep-dive explanation of a specific file, function, or module in the codebase
- understand-anything:understand-knowledge: Analyze a Karpathy-pattern LLM wiki knowledge base and generate an interactive knowledge graph with entity extraction, implicit relationships, and topic clustering.
- understand-anything:understand-onboard: Use when you need to generate an onboarding guide for new team members joining a project
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. ```

**The log is a no-op for ordinary events.** `packages/host-service/src/trpc/router/notifications/companion-question-sink.ts:212-221`:
```ts
export function warnDroppedCompanionCapture(
	payload: CompanionHookPayload,
	reason: string,
): void {
	if (!payload.companionQuestion && !payload.companionQuestionResolved) return;
	console.warn("[companion-capture] dropping question payload:", reason, {
```
→ A `PermissionRequest` with no companion payload is dropped **completely silently**. The hook script sees `2*` and exits 0 (`notify-hook.template.sh:141-143`); the Python logs `"action": "posted"` with `httpStatus: 200` (`pane-map-hook.ts:2310-2314`) — **the log says "posted" for a dropped event**.

`origin_workspace_id` is nullable with `onDelete: "set null"` — `packages/host-service/src/db/schema.ts:20-23`:
```ts
originWorkspaceId: text("origin_workspace_id").references(
    () => workspaces.id,
    { onDelete: "set null" },
),
```
Set only on terminal open/upsert: `packages/host-service/src/terminal/terminal.ts:1579`, `:1586`.

---

# 3. Renderer subscription + gating

**Subscribe** — `HostNotificationSubscriber.tsx:64-83`:
```ts
const bus = getEventBus(hostUrl, () => getHostServiceWsToken(hostUrl));
const removeAgentListener = bus.on(
    "agent:lifecycle",
    "*",
    handleAgentLifecycle,
);
```
Per **host URL**, not per workspace. `"*"` → no bus-level workspace filter (`packages/workspace-client/src/lib/eventBus.ts:178-184`). `useEffect` deps `[hostUrl]` only, handler is `useEffectEvent` → no stale closure.

**Gate 1 — workspace must be in this subscriber's list.** `HostNotificationSubscriber.tsx:41-54`:
```ts
const workspace = workspacesById.get(workspaceId);
if (!workspace) return;
handleV2AgentLifecycleEvent({ ... });
```
**Silent. No logging.** (Contrast: the Electron fallback path logs its equivalent drop — `V2NotificationController.tsx:169-180`, `reason: "workspace-not-loaded"`.)

**Gate 2 — sidebar visibility filter.** `V2NotificationController.tsx:103-116`:
```ts
const workspaceHosts = useMemo(
    () =>
        allWorkspaceHosts.filter((workspace) =>
            visibleWorkspaceIds.has(workspace.workspaceId),
        ),
```
`useVisibleSidebarWorkspaceIds.ts:73-90` — a workspace is visible only if (a) it has a local-state row, is not `isHidden`, **and its `projectId` is in the sidebar-projects set**; or (b) it's a `type === "main"` workspace auto-included on this machine (`sidebarVisibility.ts:33-49`). Notably `useVisibleSidebarWorkspaceIds.ts:37-40` requires the sidebar project to also exist in live `hostProjects`.

**Gate 3 — host-group routing.** `V2NotificationController.tsx:289-315` / `:323-340`:
```ts
if (machineId && hostId === machineId) {
    return activeHostUrl;
}
return `${relayUrl}/hosts/${buildHostRoutingKey(organizationId, hostId)}`;
```
`:297` `if (!hostUrl) continue;` — if `activeHostUrl` is null the workspace lands in **no** group at all.

**No eventType filter, no dedupe, no seen-cursor, no sequence/ordering check before the call.** `paneLayout` being null does **not** drop: `getNotificationWorkspaceStatesById` uses `?? null` (`:256`, `:266`) and `resolveV2NotificationTarget` falls back to a tabless target (`resolveV2NotificationTarget.ts:24-33`).

**Gating inside** `handleV2AgentLifecycleEvent` (`lifecycleEvents.ts:61-100`) — status update always runs first (`:66`); only the **chime + native notification** are gated:
```ts
if (
    payload.eventType === "Start" ||
    payload.eventType === "Attached" ||
    payload.eventType === "Detached" ||
    payload.eventType === "BackgroundRunning" ||
    payload.eventType === "SubagentActive"
) {
    return;
}
if (shouldSuppress(target, paneLayout)) return;
```
`shouldSuppress` (`:344-356`) suppresses only when window focused **and** target pane visible. `PermissionRequest` is not in the early-return list → chimes.

---

# 4. Throttle / dedupe / rate-limit on the path

**None anywhere** — no rate limiter on `/trpc/*` (`app.ts:282-305`), no `lastEventType ===` suppression, no `occurredAt < lastEventAt` guard.

Closest things:

- `store.ts:64-114` (host `TerminalAgentStore.recordEvent`) records `lastEventAt`/`lastEventType` but **never compares** — no suppression. `:81` `if (!agentId && !existing) return;` drops only when no agentId has ever been seen for that terminal.
- `markTerminalSeen` is monotonic — `apps/desktop/src/renderer/stores/v2-notifications/store.ts:250-254`:
  ```ts
  // Monotonic: a late event must not roll the seen mark back.
  const bumpSeen = prev === undefined || prev < at;
  ```
  Affects the seen cursor only, not delivery.
- Python-side red guard `pane-map-hook.ts:1507-1510` **rewrites** clearing events to `SubagentActive`; it does not suppress `PermissionRequest`.
- Repeated `PermissionRequest` for the same terminal is idempotent, not suppressed — `statusTransitions.ts:90-95` returns `set: ["permission"]`; `applySourceAxes` just restamps `axes[axis] = occurredAt` (`store.ts:373`).

---

# 5. Why ONE terminal's `PermissionRequest` drops while others deliver

Ranked, all workspace-scoped and all silent:

**(a) `originWorkspaceId` is NULL for that one terminal** — `notifications.ts:107-113`. Happens when the owning workspace row was deleted (`onDelete: "set null"`, `schema.ts:22`) or the terminal row predates/missed the workspace upsert. Other terminals in other workspaces resolve fine. Returns 200, logs nothing.

**(b) That workspace is not in `visibleSidebarWorkspaceIds`** — `V2NotificationController.tsx:105-108` → workspace absent from `workspacesById` → `HostNotificationSubscriber.tsx:44` `if (!workspace) return;`. Triggers: `sidebarState.isHidden === true`, its `projectId` not in the user's sidebar projects, or the project missing from live `hostProjects` (`useVisibleSidebarWorkspaceIds.ts:37-40, 73-77`). Host still broadcasts; only the renderer drops. **Zero logging.**

**(c) Host-group mismatch** — workspace's `hostId !== machineId` puts it in the relay group only (`V2NotificationController.tsx:339`), while its terminal's events arrive on the local `activeHostUrl` subscriber whose `workspaces` list excludes it → `:44` drop. Or `activeHostUrl === null` → `:297` `continue` → no subscriber.

**(d) Foreign-workspace axis guard (dot only, not delivery)** — `store.ts:367-369`:
```ts
const foreign =
    prev !== undefined && prev.workspaceId !== workspaceId;
if (foreign && ops.set.length === 0) return;
```
A re-homed terminal whose store entry carries a stale `workspaceId` blocks **clear-only** ops. `PermissionRequest` has `set: ["permission"]`, so it passes — this cannot drop the red, but it can strand a red set under an old workspaceId.

**(e) Unmapped eventType** — `map-event-type.ts:118` `return null`. If the terminal's agent emits a permission variant outside the `:87-98` list (e.g. a Codex/Gemini/Copilot-specific name), that one terminal's reds vanish while others map fine. `notifications.ts:88-94`, 200, no log.

---

## Notable

The Electron fallback in `V2NotificationController.tsx:188-196` calls `markV2AgentLifecycleTargetSeen` — **not** `handleV2AgentLifecycleEvent`. That path updates dots but never chimes or shows a native notification (`lifecycleEvents.ts:108-128`). It also re-POSTs to `notifications.hook` (`:200-212`), so a drop at the host is re-attempted from the renderer only for that fallback path.</result>

# OPEN (2026-08-06, not yet investigated — user interrupted, said "save context")

Two user reports from screenshot of live Superset sidebar (workspace `superset arm64 - master`, tab "Claude Resume"):

## Bug 1: AskUser pending but dot YELLOW not red
- Pane shows active AskUserQuestion overlay ("Fold ADB", 5 options, "Enter to select") — unanswered.

- Key context in same pane: "1 monitor still running", multiple bg-command-completed notifications ("Watch sideload", "Verify APK freshness ... exit code 0"). So Monitor/background task-notifications were landing while the question sat pending.

**Prime hypothesis (MONITOR-STOMP):** a monitor/bg task-notification re-invokes the agent mid-pending-AskUser → hook events from that resumed turn (Start/UserPromptSubmit-shaped, or Stop at turn end) clear the latched `permission` axis even though the question is still unanswered → display falls back to working-yellow (bg hold keeps it yellow). Harness explicitly delivers monitor events during pending AskUser ("events... are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question"). Prior fixed class was mirror-stomp (SUBTOOL-RED); this would be a NEW stomp path via monitor wake-ups.
- Alternate: the red-latching POST for this AskUser never arrived (hook failure — see [[project_arm64_git_bash_hook_crash]]).

**Diagnose FIRST, before code:** read `~/.superset/logs/dot-decisions.log` (always-on, first stop per [[reference_codex_cli_and_dots_logging]]) + `agent-dot-render.log` (renderer truth) around the AskUser timestamp — find whether permission latched then cleared (which event cleared it), or never latched.

- Sidebar branch row shows chips "Claude Resume" + "Claude" (per-terminal, correct), then a SEPARATE row below with red-starburst icon + "2".

# Bug 1 ROOT-CAUSED (2026-08-06): DEAD-BUS lost-event — NOT monitor-stomp, NOT hook failure

Pending AskUserQuestion showed yellow because the renderer's WS event bus to host-service was **dead 00:47→08:30 UTC (7h43m)**; the PermissionRequest red (03:45Z, terminal `8b693144-c721-4791-bedc-591a136d5b42`, session `41b65f55-...`) landed inside the window and evaporated (fire-and-forget broadcast, zero clients = destroyed). Dot froze at pre-outage `working`.

Evidence (dot-diagnosis agent, verified):
- Hook side PERFECT: dot-decisions.log has both RED lines at 03:45Z (PreToolUse:AskUserQuestion + Notification); agent-notify-hook.log `"posted"` 200; `.askq/_main` marker still present; transcript ends at AskUserQuestion, no tool_result.
- Renderer: `agent-dot-render.log.prev` snapshots byte-identical 00:47:32Z→08:30:22Z; 15s after the red POST still `working`. Three OTHER events for same terminal (2× BackgroundRunning, 1 Stop GREEN) also never applied in-window → transport, not axis logic.
- Trigger: host-service restarted 00:54:58Z (new host dir 00:55:02Z); desktop app never restarted (up since 05/08).
- No self-heal: blocked agent emits no further hook events → nothing re-asserts the axis. Same class store.ts:218-227 documents for the (BA) blue axis; permission is WORSE (blocked agent has no next turn).
- MONITOR-STOMP disproved: SubagentActive clears nothing (statusTransitions.ts:64-74); only Start/Detached/terminal-fallthrough clear permission; none fired post-03:45Z.

Code holes:
- `packages/host-service/src/events/event-bus.ts:146,171` — fire-and-forget broadcast, no queue/persistence.
- `packages/workspace-client/src/lib/eventBus.ts:277` `maxEnqueuedMessages: 0`; `:287-291` reconnect replays ONLY `fs:watch` — no agent-lifecycle backfill/state resync.
- `apps/desktop/src/renderer/lib/host-service-auth.ts:34` — in-memory PSK cache; restarted host issues NEW PSK → stale token → `ACCESS_DENIED_RETRY_MS` 5-min loop (`eventBus.ts:129`) plausibly explains 7.5h outage. **INFERRED link — confirm during fix.**

FIX DIRECTION: make red re-assertable, not edge-dependent — on every bus `open`, renderer requests per-terminal agent-state snapshot from host (durable truth incl. `.askq` markers) and reconciles axes; refresh PSK on reconnect; visible "notifications disconnected" indicator so a dead bus stops looking like healthy dots.

Transition map: `.../V2NotificationController/lib/statusTransitions.ts` (PermissionRequest → set:["permission"] at :90-95; SubagentActive sets working and clears nothing :64-74; Start :76-88 and Detached :48-62 clear permission).
- Host-side durable truth: `packages/host-service/src/terminal-agents/store.ts:64-114` `recordEvent` keeps per-terminal `agentId`/`lastEventType`/`lastEventAt`; the Python hook additionally maintains pending-question marker dirs `~/.superset/agent-subagent-running/<terminalId>.askq/` (with `_main` file) — and the Python-side red guard (embedded template in `apps/desktop/src/main/lib/agent-jsonl-watcher/pane-map-hook.ts:1507-1510`) rewrites red-clearing events to SubagentActive while a question marker is present, which means `lastEventType` ALONE loses the permission truth (it may read SubagentActive while a question is pending). So the snapshot must include marker-derived pending-permission state, not just lastEventType.

1. **Host snapshot procedure** (host-service tRPC, near the notifications router): returns for every current terminal-agent binding: terminalId, originWorkspaceId, agentId, lastEventType, lastEventAt, plus `pendingPermission: boolean` derived from the `.askq` marker presence for that terminal (apply the same staleness/self-heal conventions existing marker readers use — search for how `.askq`/`agent-subagent-running` markers are read elsewhere, e.g. MARKER-RECONCILE, and stay consistent). 3. **PSK refresh**: on an access-denied close, invalidate the cached token and re-obtain a fresh one before the next retry (per your confirmed reading of the auth flow), so a host restart cannot strand the socket for hours. Keep the retry loop bounded/backoff-sane.
4. **Disconnected indicator**: minimal, theme-consistent visible state when the agent-notification bus for the active host is not connected (e.g. small warning pill/dot in the sidebar footer or near the workspace header — pick the least invasive existing surface; no new dependency). Must disappear on reconnect.
5. **FEATURES.md**: add feature entry + marker `(BUS-RESYNC)` following the file's exact existing conventions (marker line is TAB-separated in the fenced markers block), and place the marker token in a survivable code comment at the resync seam. Same commit. Do NOT touch the version or any other feature rows.

COMMIT (local only, do not push): conventional title `fix(desktop,host-service): resync agent dots on event-bus reconnect (BUS-RESYNC)`. Body: DEAD-BUS class — host restart killed WS bus 7h43m, events fire-and-forget, reconnect replayed only fs:watch, stale PSK kept socket in 5-min denied loop (confirmed/refuted per your finding); fix = snapshot reconcile on open + token refresh + disconnected indicator. Three independent pieces of evidence, each sufficient alone:

1. packages/workspace-client/src/lib/primeRelayAffinity.ts:28-29 — the _whoowns preflight returns null for any URL that is not /hosts/<id>/*. A local bus dials http://127.0.0.1:<port>/events, so no probe runs, `probe?.status === 403` is never true, and ACCESS_DENIED_RETRY_MS (the 5-minute loop at eventBus.ts:129) is UNREACHABLE on a loopback host. That loop only applies to relay-fronted hosts, which authenticate with the user JWT, not a PSK.

2. packages/host-service/src/app.ts:255-264 — the local /events wsAuth middleware answers a bad token with 401, not 403. Even if the probe ran, relaySocket.ts:12-18 documents 401 as the self-healing case precisely because getToken is re-read.

3. packages/workspace-client/src/lib/relaySocket/relaySocket.ts:68-70 — the URL provider awaits opts.getToken() before EVERY dial, and eventBus.ts passes `() => getHostServiceWsToken(hostUrl)`, which reads the secrets Map live. No dial can reuse a cached token. Additionally LocalHostServiceProvider.tsx:149-153 and :224-226 poll hostServiceCoordinator.getConnection every 5s and rewrite the secret, and the coordinator serves the live instance.secret (host-service-coordinator.ts:362-368).

Conclusion: the socket was never stranded in a denied loop. It was reconnecting normally into a bus with no backfill — the dots were dead because the EVENTS were destroyed, not because the socket was.

COMMIT: one commit on main, local only, title `fix(desktop,host-service): harden BUS-RESYNC reconcile per review (BUS-RESYNC)`. Body lists F1-F8 one line each. `git commit -F <file>` for the message.

RETURN: per-finding what you changed (file:line), verification summary, commit sha, and anything you deliberately deviated on (with reason).

input.prompt:
READ-ONLY investigation in "C:\Users\khair\Code Projects\fork-superset-windows-arm64" (Superset desktop fork, Windows ARM64). Another agent is editing renderer files concurrently — do NOT edit anything; prefer `git show HEAD:<path>` / `MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1 git show` for committed content when a working-tree file looks mid-edit.

PROVEN FACTS (from live diagnosis today, 2026-08-06, host.db + logs):
- Workspace f85bc39c ("DCB1596", type main) pane held terminal `795ee9f0` — properly registered (terminal_sessions row), agent hook events flowed, dot worked (10:27:45Z).
- At 10:28:12Z the host set `dispose_requested_at` then `ended_at` on 795ee9f0.
- The pane then held a NEW terminal id `fc7ffd00-e02b-4788-b478-2db7f61ee171` with ZERO rows ever in terminal_sessions, ZERO in terminal_agent_bindings, ZERO mentions in host-service.log. The Claude session's pane-map file `~/.superset/session-pane-map/824c4068-*.json` maps to fc7ffd00.
- Every superset-notify.py POST for fc7ffd00 hit the unknown-terminal guard in `packages/host-service/src/trpc/router/notifications/notifications.ts:105-117` → silent `{success:true, ignored:true}` 200 for 22 minutes (no broadcast, no binding).
- The pane's TerminalConnectionIndicator showed red "Disconnected" (`apps/desktop/src/renderer/.../TerminalConnectionIndicator.tsx:156-167`): transport `gaveUp` — the terminal-host WS attach failed because the host has no session fc7ffd00.
- At 10:50 the dot reappeared ONLY via the Electron fallback path (V2NotificationController.handleElectronAgentLifecycle, pane-map-resolved), which paints the store locally; its re-POST to notifications.hook was still dropped.

QUESTIONS TO ANSWER (with file:line evidence):
1. WHO minted fc7ffd00? Trace every code path that creates a terminal id in the renderer/desktop main and attaches a pane to it (new terminal, pane restore, dispose-then-recreate, agent-session resume, workspace reopen). Which path can produce a terminal id WITHOUT a corresponding host-side terminal_sessions insert (terminal open/upsert lives at `packages/host-service/src/terminal/terminal.ts:~1579,1586`)? Pay attention to what happens when a terminal is disposed (dispose_requested_at flow) while its pane stays open — is there a recreate/retry path that generates a fresh client-side id and only registers it on successful WS attach (which then fails → id exists renderer-side only, forever)? Also check: was 795ee9f0's dispose itself triggered by something suspicious (e.g. host-side idle reap, renderer detach) 30s after creation?
2. What is the ORDERING contract between (a) pane-map hook writing terminalId for a session, (b) host terminal_sessions insert, (c) WS attach? Identify the exact window where hooks can fire for an unregistered terminal.
3. FIX DESIGN for both approved items, concretely:
   a. `notifications.hook` fail-loud on unknown terminalId: what should it do — 4xx? log + broadcast anyway via pane-map adoption? Look at what data is available (input has terminalId + eventType + agent) and whether an ADOPTION insert (create a terminal_sessions row with originWorkspaceId resolved from the desktop pane-map, or a a dedicated adoption RPC) is feasible host-side or needs the desktop main to supply workspaceId. Recommend the minimal correct design honoring "fail fast and loud" + "DB is source of truth".
   b. Registration fix: the precise change so a pane-attached terminal is ALWAYS registered host-side before (or upon) first hook POST — e.g. make the recreate path call the same open/upsert as normal creation, or make attach-failure surface loudly instead of leaving a ghost.
4. Blast radius: what else reads terminal_sessions by terminalId and silently no-ops on miss (companion capture? kanban? auto-resume?) — list the sites so the fix can cover or at least log them.

Return a compact report: (1) the minting path with file:line, (2) the ordering window, (3) recommended fix design for a+b (specific files/functions, edge cases incl. the dispose-recreate race), (4) blast-radius list. NO code edits.

content.text:
Answer to your question, confirmed with logs: **the chat's terminal is a ghost.** Thirty seconds into that DCB1596 chat the host disposed the original terminal and the pane re-minted a new terminal id that was **never registered host-side** — so the host silently discarded every dot event (`200 ignored:true`) for 22 minutes. No yellow because nothing was ever written to the dot store. The red "Disconnected" badge in the pane corner is the same root cause: the terminal transport can't attach to a session the host doesn't have. (The yellow you do see on "July tech update" belongs to a different, healthy chat. Side fact: the workspace *icon* never shows working-yellow by design — it becomes a spinner.)

In flight now:
- `review-fixes` (Opus): the 8 review findings + new **F9** guard so the resync sweep can never clear a ghost terminal's fallback dot.
- `ghost-investigate` (Opus, read-only): tracing who mints unregistered terminal ids + the fail-loud/adoption design, per your "full fix now". Implementation follows once the hardening commit lands and the tree is free.
